1.explanation: The core of the bug lives in src/languages/typescript.js where the exported `default` function builds on the JavaScript grammar to produce TypeScript highlighting rules. It injects an INTERFACE mode (with `beginKeywords: 'interface'` and `keywords: 'interface extends'`) and then reuses the existing JS modes for everything else. However, there is no dedicated mode to match and consume a `<… extends …>` generic parameter list, so the highlighter treats the `extends` keyword as part of the normal code stream and never closes the `<` bracket, leaking the remainder of the file into that mode. The helper `swapMode` function is also involved (it swaps out other modes by label) and any incorrect replacement there can exacerbate the generics-matching issue. To fix this, the default grammar setup should introduce or correct a mode that explicitly matches TypeScript generic parameters (including nested `<…>` and `extends` clauses) so that the parser can close the generics block and continue normal tokenizing afterwards.

2.explanation: The core of the breakage lives in src/languages/typescript.js. Its INTERFACE mode only scans for “interface … extends” up until the opening brace and never accounts for the use of extends inside generic parameter lists (<T extends U>). Because generics with extends never match any active mode, the parser abandons highlighting for all subsequent tokens. The swapMode helper only swaps out existing top-level rules (shebang, use_strict) and has no bearing on generic parsing. Meanwhile, the global KEYWORDS in lib/ecmascript.js does list “extends” but, without a dedicated generic parameter rule in the TypeScript grammar, it never gets consumed correctly. Fixing this requires adding or extending a mode in typescript.js to recognize “extends” inside ‹…› so that the rest of the code remains highlighted.
2.bug_scenario: In the provided screenshots you can see that as soon as a generic type uses the “extends” keyword (for example: interface Prefixer<Something extends string> or parse<From extends string>), the syntax highlighter in highlight.js v10.3.0 stops matching any further tokens and the rest of your TypeScript code is rendered as plain text.
